title: Unique Paths
statement: A robot stands in the top-left square of a grid with m rows and n columns. It may only move one square right or one square down. Count the different routes that take it to the bottom-right square.

example.caption: A 3 by 4 grid has 10 routes. The table counts the routes into each square.

output.label: dp[i][j] = routes from the top-left to square (i, j)

idea.sentence: dp[i][j] is the number of routes into square (i, j). Every route arrives from above or from the left, so dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j] + dp[i][j-1].

jargon.plain: Solve a big question by filling a table of smaller answers, where each cell is built from cells already filled.
The cells you can fill without any recurrence. Here: the first row and first column.

watch.inputHint: Two numbers: rows m, then columns n, e.g. 3, 4

compare.unit: steps (rough; the route count grows exponentially, drawn as 2n)

rows.name: Brute force
rows.note: Walk every route with recursion. The same squares are revisited again and again.

rows.name: 2-D table
rows.note: Each square is computed once from two neighbours.

rows.name: One rolling row
rows.note: Row i only reads row i-1 and the cell to its left, so one row is enough: row[j] += row[j-1].

fast.takeaway: Count by the last move. Every route into a square ends with a step from above or a step from the left, and those two groups never overlap.

stages.title: Base row and column
stages.note: Make an m by n table. The first row and column are 1: only straight moves reach them.

stages.title: Add above and left
stages.note: Fill row by row, left to right. Each square is the square above plus the square to its left.

stages.title: Read the corner
stages.note: The bottom-right square holds the number of routes for the whole grid.

edges.title: One square
edges.why: The robot is already at the finish. The empty route counts as one.

edges.title: One row or one column
edges.why: There is no choice to make. The loops over the inside never run.

edges.title: Symmetry
edges.why: Swapping rows and columns gives the same count, so a rolling row can use the smaller side.

edges.title: Counts grow fast
edges.why: Counts grow like a binomial coefficient. Past about 2 billion a 32-bit int overflows.

gotchas.text: make([][]int, m) gives m nil rows. Allocate every row with make([]int, n) before you write into it.
Array(m).fill(Array(n).fill(1)) reuses ONE inner array for every row, so writing one cell changes all rows. Use Array.from with a callback that builds a new row.
The first row and column must start at 1, not 0. With zeros, every inside square adds zeros and the answer is 0.
int is 64-bit on most machines, so this fits. On a 32-bit target, counts past 2^31 overflow silently. Use int64 if you care.

recap.key: dp[i][j] = routes into square (i, j) = dp[i-1][j] + dp[i][j-1]. First row and column are 1.
recap.complexity: Time O(m·n). Space O(m·n), or O(n) with one rolling row.
moves: Make an m by n table of 1s
Fill row by row, left to right
